text:
Mika Zibanejad scored twice in the second period, and neither goal came easily. The first, 59 seconds in, went in on a 4% chance by our numbers, a wrist shot that barely had a right to beat Devin Cooley. The second came on the power play, a slap shot at 10:52 that made it 2-0 NYR. Zibanejad was drafted sixth overall by the Senators in 2011 out of Djurgarden, and on this night he made two modest looks count for everything.

Calgary controlled more of the game than the final score suggests. The Flames outshot New York 30-24, out-attempted them 51-48, and our deserved-to-win number (the share of simulated replays of every shot that a team wins) came out 55% for CGY and 45% for NYR. At even strength it was close, 1.61 expected goals to 1.45 in Calgary's favor. The gap in total expected goals, 3.21 for NYR to 2.21 for CGY, came largely from the third period, when New York's chances jumped to 1.8. Joonas Korpisalo saved 1.21 goals more than the quality of his shots called for, which is the real reason Calgary got one. Adam Klapka, a never-drafted free agent who worked his way up through the AHL's Calgary Wranglers, cut it to 2-1 on a power-play snap shot at 7:41 of the third.

The Flames pulled no closer. Tye Kartye finished it at 19:53 with a wrist shot on a 66% chance, set up by J.T. Miller. Calgary now has to find a way to turn its edge in play into goals, while New York leaves Alberta with the win on the back of its goalie.
